messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Marisol Vega had always described herself as someone who could be counted on in a crisis. At 48, the single social ministry worker moved through North American church basements, community kitchens, and parish offices with the practical steadiness that her colleagues and clients relied on. The accident that changed that steadiness happened on an ordinary afternoon when she was riding as a passenger in a car, returning from a home visit. Another vehicle came out of nowhere at an intersection and hit them hard enough to leave her shaken, pinned by the sudden violence of it and the complete loss of control. In the moments immediately after, what stayed with her most was not only the crash itself but the feeling of being physically trapped in a body she could not command. When others told her to stay calm and assured her she was safe, she could not quite believe them. The scene returned to her later in fragments that felt abruptly close, especially the image of cars struck in accidents, metal buckling and bodies jolted without warning. Even now, that kind of image could surface in her mind while she was trying to make coffee or standing in line at work, arriving with the same force as if it were happening again.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol began arranging her life around the fear of another sudden loss of control. She stopped driving altogether and refused rides when she could manage it, even if taking a vehicle would have made her workday easier. Instead, she walked farther, waited longer, and sometimes left a place early rather than risk being a passenger. Her ministry work took her to scattered sites across the city, but she increasingly chose assignments that did not require travel, or found reasons to join meetings by phone rather than in person. That change narrowed her world in practical ways, and she was aware of it, yet the thought of being in a car brought back the same conviction that she could be harmed before she could do anything about it. She had come to believe that bad things could happen to her without warning and that her own efforts could not stop them. That sense of helplessness was especially sharp when she was asked to depend on someone else’s schedule or judgment; being forced to do something, even something ordinary, could leave her tense and angry in a way that surprised people who knew her as gentle and composed.

At work, Marisol’s attention kept drifting to exits the moment she entered a room or building. In a parish hall, at a food pantry, or while sitting in a counselor’s office, she quietly mapped the nearest door and watched where people were standing, as though a quick route out might spare her from being cornered again. She told herself she was simply being careful, but she knew she was scanning. Even when colleagues reassured her that the setting was safe, she found it impossible to settle fully into that reassurance. Her body did not cooperate with her intention to relax. She avoided lying down after work, avoided resting too long on weekends, and resisted anything that left her feeling physically unprepared, as if letting her guard down might invite another blow. If she became tired, lightheaded, or physically strained, she grew uneasy, because feeling ill or depleted made her think of her body as unreliable and vulnerable. What frightened her most was not only the memory of the crash but the possibility that her own body might fail her without warning, leaving her unable to protect herself or even understand what was happening until it was too late.

Ordinary sounds could also set her off. A door slamming in the ministry office, a sudden bang from a dropped pan in the shelter kitchen, the sharp horn of a car outside the building could make her jump before she had time to think. The startle was brief, but it left her embarrassed and keyed up, as if her nerves were always waiting for another impact. Over time, she had built a life that looked orderly from the outside but was increasingly organized around caution. She avoided driving, avoided relaxing, avoided putting her body under stress, and kept a careful watch on every unfamiliar room. By the time she sought help, what brought her in was the exhaustion of maintaining that vigilance while still trying to serve others. She wanted to keep doing her work and move through the city without feeling hunted by the possibility of another accident. More than anything, she hoped for some way to trust her body and her surroundings again, though she feared that what happened to her had permanently changed the rules of safety and left her at the mercy of forces she could never fully control.
